title: Our account rules: size, caps and grades
teaches: Our sizing rules as one list: shares come from the account, the risk percent and the stop, rounded down, then the smaller of that and the 40% cap, bought at one price with one stop; the setup's grade picks the risk (A+ 1% to 1.5%, A and B 0.5% to 1%, B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%, new traders 0.25%); we trade stocks at $10 or more doing $20 million a day, never over 1% of a stock's volume; the book runs to 100% of the account, or 200% on margin only when our market reading is Green; 2x and 3x ETFs are preferred; the same stock gets 3 tries a week and 6 a month; and the account is recalculated weekly or monthly.

sources.why_reliable: The Van Tharp Institute's own page setting out Dr. Van K. Tharp's position-sizing teaching (Ph.D. in psychology, decades as a trading coach, author of The Definitive Guide to Position Sizing, interviewed in Schwager's Market Wizards). F9.01 files it under the contract's 'named author with a known record' clause; used here only for 'start small' and 'size from the growing account', never for a key on its own.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap (A7, or the ladder's cap in a drawdown, A8).
facts.claim: Our rule: shares are the account times the risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then the smaller of that and the position cap.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: Our rule: buy the full position at one price with one stop; never scale in or add.

facts.quote: A7. Max position 40% of the account (raised from 20-25% on 2026-11-09: "RAISE THE CAP TO 40% ACTUALLY. ESPECIALLY WITH EARLY TRIMS AT 3-5R THAT IS FINE.").
facts.claim: Our max position is 40% of the account, raised on 2026-11-09 from the old 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: A tight stop never justifies a bigger position than that: a gap can jump the stop.
facts.claim: A tight stop never earns a position above the cap, because a gap can jump the stop.

facts.quote: All positions together: up to 200% of the account in a Green market (margin, B24, F60), up to 100% otherwise; so a full book of 10 averages about 20% a position.
facts.claim: The whole book can reach 200% of the account in a Green market on margin, 100% otherwise, so ten full positions average about 20% each.

facts.quote: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%": the stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy (a loss on the position, not the account).
facts.claim: Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy price; that 3% is a loss on the position, not the account.

facts.quote: Setup grades set the size: A and B setups at normal size; A+ sized up; B- or lower sized down.
facts.claim: The setup's grade sets the size: A and B normal, A+ bigger, B- or lower smaller.

facts.quote: Risk by grade: A+ 1% to 1.5%; A and B 0.5% to 1%; B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%.
facts.claim: Risk by grade: A+ 1% to 1.5% of the account, A and B 0.5% to 1%, B- or lower 0.25% to 0.5%.

facts.quote: Grading a setup (A+, A, B, B-) is discretionary and hard to define; no fixed checklist is taught as ours.
facts.claim: Grading a setup is a judgment call; we teach no fixed checklist.

facts.quote: New traders start at 0.25% risk per trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules, then size up.
facts.claim: New traders risk 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades have followed the rules.

facts.quote: Trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
facts.claim: We trade only stocks priced $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not watched at all.

facts.quote: Margin: total long positions up to 200% of the account. Risk per trade is still a percent of the account.
facts.claim: On margin the long book can reach 200% of the account, but risk per trade is still a percent of the account.

facts.quote: Margin (up to 200%, B24) is used only in a Green market.
facts.claim: Margin is used only when our market reading is Green.

facts.quote: Leveraged ETFs are preferred; no extra rules.
facts.claim: 2x and 3x ETFs are preferred under our rules, with no extra rules for them.

facts.quote: The same stock: at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
facts.claim: The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.

facts.quote: Recalculate the account value weekly or monthly and size every trade from it.
facts.claim: Recalculate the account value weekly or monthly and size every trade from that number.

facts.quote: Risking the same percent on every trade is also fine: pick one way and write it in the plan.
facts.claim: A flat risk percent on every trade is also fine; pick one way and write it in your plan.

facts.quote: Under 1% is normal; 1.5% is the most any grade uses (E49); 2% is the absolute ceiling.
facts.claim: Under 1% risk is normal, 1.5% is the most any grade uses, and 2% is the absolute ceiling.

facts.quote: Never raise risk past the rules after a run of winners.
facts.claim: A run of winners never raises your risk past the rules.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: Stop first, a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low; size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip.

facts.quote: A market filter decides when the account trades: the app's market reading (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red).
facts.claim: The app's market reading (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) is our market filter.

facts.quote: A “margin account” is a type of brokerage account in which the broker-dealer lends the investor cash, using the account as collateral, to purchase securities.
facts.claim: In a margin account the broker lends you cash against the account to buy securities.

facts.quote: Margin increases investors’ purchasing power, but also exposes investors to the potential for larger losses.
facts.claim: Margin raises your buying power and your possible losses.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: Once triggered, a stop is a market order and can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: A stock’s liquidity generally refers to how rapidly shares of a stock can be bought or sold without substantially impacting the stock price.
facts.claim: A stock's liquidity is how fast its shares can be bought or sold without moving the price much.

facts.quote: Stocks with low liquidity may be difficult to sell and may cause you to take a bigger loss if you cannot sell the shares when you want to.
facts.claim: A stock with low liquidity can be hard to sell and can hand you a bigger loss.

facts.quote: Limit orders are a particularly valuable tool for trading thinly traded securities, where even small orders have the potential to represent a high percentage of an ETF's average daily volume and, as a result, impact the prevailing market price.
facts.claim: In a thinly traded security, even a small order can be a large share of average daily volume and move the price.

facts.quote: Leveraged ETFs seek to deliver multiples of the daily performance of the index or benchmark they track.
facts.claim: A 2x or 3x ETF aims for a multiple of its index's daily move.

facts.quote: For example, a 2x leveraged S&P 500 ETF seeks to deliver twice the investment return of the S&P 500 Index. This also means that this ETF will lose 2% for every 1% loss in the index.
facts.claim: A 2x S&P 500 ETF loses 2% for every 1% the index loses.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Shares come from dividing the dollars you will risk by the risk per share: $500 over $20 is 25 shares.

facts.quote: For a general rule, some traders may risk up to 1%–2% of their account on a single trade and allocate up to 5%–10% of their portfolio in any single position.
facts.claim: Schwab's general rule: risk 1% to 2% a trade and put 5% to 10% of the portfolio in one position.

facts.quote: It’s best to start small (very small) and minimize the “tuition paid” to learn the new strategy.
facts.claim: Start very small to keep the cost of learning low.

facts.quote: You can risk more as your portfolio gets bigger, but you only risk 1% of your total portfolio on any one idea.
facts.claim: With a fixed percent, dollar risk grows with the account while the percent stays the same.

facts.quote: Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: Our market reading guides risk: Green full risk per grade, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups, Red mostly cash and shorts.

walkthroughs.title: Size from the stop, then cap it
steps: Stop first. Then shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down.
Then the cap. The size is the SMALLER of that and 40% of the account.
A tight stop never earns more than the cap. A gap can jump any stop.
Buy the full size at one price with one stop. No scaling in, no adding.

walkthroughs.title: The grade sets the risk
steps: Grade the setup first: A+, A, B, B- or lower. That's a judgment call. We teach no checklist for it.
A+ risks 1% to 1.5% of the account. A and B, 0.5% to 1%. B- or lower, 0.25% to 0.5%.
2% is the absolute ceiling. New traders start at 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules.
Risking the same percent every trade is fine too. Pick one way and write it in your plan.

walkthroughs.title: What we trade, and how much of it
steps: Stocks at $10 or more, trading at least $20 million a day. Never more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.
The book: 100% of the account, or 200% on margin in a Green market. At 200%, ten positions average about 20% each.
2x and 3x ETFs are preferred, no extra rules. The same stock gets 3 tries a week, 6 a month.
Recalculate the account weekly or monthly and size every trade from it.

questions.q: Under our rule, what sets your share count before the cap check?
choices: How strongly you like the setup
questions.why: Account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop). That gives the number of shares that lose your planned risk if the stop is hit. Round down, never up. Then compare it with the 40% cap and take the smaller size. The stop comes first; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, then the math: account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then the cap.

wrong.Account × risk % ÷ the share price: That divides by the price, so the stop is not in it. Divide by entry minus stop, the risk per share.
wrong.Account × 40% ÷ the share price: That's the 40% cap, a ceiling. The risk math comes first, and the cap only limits it.
wrong.How strongly you like the setup: Liking it feeds the grade, and the grade picks the risk percent. The share count still comes from the stop.

questions.simple: Shares come from the account times your risk percent, divided by the entry-to-stop distance. So the stop sets the count.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5)
Investopedia (s7, f09) unreachable from this machine; the key also rests on the house fact h01

questions.q: Our max position in one stock is 40% of the account.
questions.why: True. Our max position in one stock is 40% of the account. It was 20% to 25% until 2026-11-09, when we raised it. It is a ceiling, not a target. The size is the smaller of the risk math and the cap. In a drawdown, our drawdown ladder's cap applies instead.
questions.lesson_line: One stock, 40% of the account at most. The smaller of the risk math and the cap wins.
questions.simple: True, 40% of the account is the most one stock can be. The final size never goes past it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)
a number that changed recently: the cap went from 20-25% to 40% on 2026-11-09
fixed before (owner named; range misread)

questions.q: Fill in our rule.
questions.sentence: Under our rules, the most an A+ setup risks is ___ of the account.
questions.why: 1.5%. An A+ setup risks 1% to 1.5% of the account, so 1.5% is its top. It is also the most any grade uses. 2% is the absolute ceiling, and no grade uses it. 1% is the bottom of the A+ range.
questions.lesson_line: A+ gets 1% to 1.5%. No grade uses more than 1.5%.
questions.simple: It is 1.5%, the top of the A+ range of 1% to 1.5%, and the most any grade uses.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, A1)
a house number the owner set and already lowered once (E49: 'a little smaller')

questions.q: Our market reading is Green, and a setup grades B- or lower. What's our risk range for it?
questions.why: 0.25% to 0.5% of the account. The grade sets the size. A and B are normal at 0.5% to 1%. A+ is sized up to 1% to 1.5%. In a Green market, B- or lower is sized down, not skipped. In an Orange market, only A+ setups are taken.
questions.lesson_line: Lower grade, smaller risk. B- or lower gets 0.25% to 0.5%.

wrong.0.5% to 1%: That's the A and B range, normal size. B- or lower is sized down from there.
wrong.1% to 1.5%: That's the A+ range, sized up. A B- setup gets the smallest risk, not the biggest.
wrong.Skip it: A Green market takes full risk per grade. B- or lower is sized down to 0.25% to 0.5%, not skipped.

questions.simple: B- or lower risks 0.25% to 0.5%, because in a Green market a weaker setup is sized down, not skipped.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, D38)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: A tight stop lets you take a position bigger than our 40% cap.
questions.why: False. A tight stop never justifies a position bigger than the 40% cap. A gap can jump the stop. A triggered stop becomes a market order, and it can fill far from your stop price. So size from the stop, cap it at 40% of the account, and take the smaller.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop changes the share count, never the cap. A gap can jump any stop.
questions.simple: False, a tight stop changes your share count but never lifts you past the 40% cap. A gap can jump the stop.

deeper.counter: A stop just under your entry makes the share math huge. But a gap can jump the stop. Once the stop price is reached, the stop becomes a market order and can fill far below it. The 40% cap limits how much one gap can cost.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)
a number that changed recently (the 40% cap, 2026-11-09)

questions.q: We trade stocks at $10 or more. How much do they have to trade each day?
choices: At least 20 million shares a day
questions.why: At least $20 million a day. That is the second test, next to a price of $10 or more, and a stock must pass both. Liquidity is how fast shares can be bought or sold without moving the price much. A thin stock can be hard to sell and hand you a bigger loss. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: $10 or more, $20 million a day or more. Thin stocks aren't on our list.

wrong.At least $2 million a day: Too thin. Our floor is $20 million a day, ten times that.
wrong.At least $10 million a day: $10 is our price floor, not a volume number. A stock must trade at least $20 million a day.
wrong.At least 20 million shares a day: Our test counts dollars, not shares. A stock must trade at least $20 million a day.

questions.simple: Our stocks must trade at least $20 million a day, so you can get in and out without moving the price much.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Under our rules, a new trader risks 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades have followed the rules.
questions.why: True. New traders start at 0.25% risk per trade. After 50 journaled trades that followed the rules, they size up. The count is of journaled trades that followed the rules, not any 50 trades. Starting very small keeps the cost of learning low.
questions.lesson_line: New trader: 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades followed the rules.
questions.simple: True, a new trader risks 0.25% a trade until 50 journaled trades have followed the rules, so early mistakes stay cheap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C37)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: How do we grade a setup A+, A, B or B-?
choices: A judgment call, no set checklist
A points checklist that adds up
By how tight the stop is
By how high the share price is
questions.answer: A judgment call, no set checklist
questions.why: A judgment call, no set checklist. Grading a setup A+, A, B or B- is discretionary and hard to define, and we teach no fixed checklist as ours. The grade then sets the size: A and B normal, A+ sized up, B- or lower sized down. The grade picks the risk percent; the stop distance turns it into shares.
questions.lesson_line: Grading is a judgment call. The grade picks the risk; the stop picks the shares.

wrong.A points checklist that adds up: We teach no fixed checklist. The grade is a judgment call.
wrong.By how tight the stop is: The stop sets the share count, not the grade. A tight stop doesn't make a setup A+.
wrong.By how high the share price is: Price decides whether a stock is tradable ($10 or more), not how good the setup is.

questions.simple: Grading is a judgment call with no set checklist, and the grade then picks how much you risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E50, D38)

questions.q: Account $50,000, risk 1%. Entry $40, stop $38.30. Under our rule, how many shares?
questions.why: 294 shares. 1% of $50,000 is the dollars you will risk. Divide that by the distance from the $40 entry to the $38.30 stop. The math leaves a fraction of a share, so round down, never up. Then check the cap: 294 shares at $40 is well under 40% of $50,000, so the risk size stands.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk divided by the stop distance. Round down. Then check the cap.
questions.simple: You buy 294 shares: 1% of $50,000 over the distance from $40 to $38.30, rounded down, well under the cap.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
a computed key

questions.q: Account $50,000, risk 1%. Entry $50, stop $49.50. Under our rules, how many shares do you buy?
questions.why: 400 shares. The risk math alone would put the whole account in one stock: 1% of $50,000 over the distance from $50 to $49.50. The cap wins: 40% of $50,000 at the $50 entry is 400 shares. The size is always the smaller of the two. You end up risking less than the 1% you planned, and that's fine.
questions.lesson_line: Risk math, then the cap. The smaller number is your size.
questions.simple: You buy 400 shares, because the risk math wants the whole account and the 40% cap is smaller.

deeper.trap: The trap is the tight stop. Half a dollar of risk per share makes the share math huge. A gap can jump a stop that close, and a triggered stop can fill far from its price. That is why the cap, not the stop, sets this size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7)
a computed key
fixed before (the question led with 'Our 40% cap applies')

questions.q: Account $80,000. The setup is an A and you use the top of its range. How many dollars are at risk?
questions.why: $800. An A setup risks 0.5% to 1% of the account, and the top of that range is 1%. 1% of $80,000 is $800. That is your planned loss if the stop fills at its price.
questions.lesson_line: The grade picks the percent, the percent picks the dollars.
questions.simple: $800 is at risk, because the top of the A range is 1%, and 1% of $80,000 is $800.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49)
a computed key

questions.q: A stock trades 4 million shares a day on average. Under our rule, what's the most shares you may own?
questions.why: 40,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, and 1% of 4 million shares is 40,000. We read volume here as shares traded. The $20 million a day test is a separate dollar test. Own more and your own orders can move the price, going in and coming out.
questions.lesson_line: Never more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. Your exit has to fit too.
questions.simple: You may own up to 40,000 shares, because we never hold more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)
a computed key
the share-volume reading of D42 still awaits the owner's confirmation (conflicts line)

questions.story: Account $100,000. An A+ setup, so you pick 1.5% risk. Entry $20, stop $19.70, a 1.5% stop. The risk math says $100,000 in the stock.
questions.q: How big is the position?
questions.why: $40,000. The risk math says $100,000, the whole account. The cap says 40% of $100,000, which is $40,000. The smaller number wins. You end up risking less than the 1.5% you planned, and that's fine.
questions.lesson_line: The cap binds before the grade. Size from the stop, then take the smaller number.

wrong.$100,000: That's the risk math with no cap. The whole account in one stock is one gap away from a big loss.
wrong.$1,500: That's the dollars at risk, 1.5% of $100,000, not the size of the position.
wrong.$25,000: That's the old cap, 25% of the account. We raised it to 40% on 2026-11-09.

questions.simple: The position is $40,000, because the 40% cap is smaller than the $100,000 the risk math asks for.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7, E49)
a computed key

questions.q: On margin, your risk per trade becomes a percent of your buying power instead of your account.
questions.why: False. Margin lets the whole book reach 200% of the account, and only when our market reading is Green. Risk per trade is still a percent of the account. Margin raises buying power, and it also raises the size of possible losses.
questions.lesson_line: Margin changes what the book can hold, never what one trade may lose.
questions.simple: False, on margin your risk per trade is still a percent of your account, not of your buying power.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B24, F60)
a house number the owner set (200%)

questions.story: A friend shows you a B- setup, nothing special. He's risking 1.5% on it, his A+ rate, because he wants a big month.
questions.q: What do our rules say about his risk?
questions.why: Cut it to 0.25% to 0.5%. A B- or lower setup is sized down. 1% to 1.5% is the A+ range, and wanting a big month does not raise a grade. 2% is our absolute ceiling, and no grade uses it.
questions.lesson_line: The grade picks the risk, not the mood. B- gets 0.25% to 0.5%.

wrong.1.5% is fine, risk is risk: 1.5% is the A+ range. A B- setup at an A+ rate is our grade ladder upside down.
wrong.Raise it to 2%, the ceiling: 2% is the absolute ceiling, and no grade uses it. 1.5% is the most any grade gets, and only A+.
wrong.Lower it to 1%, normal size: 1% is the top of the A and B range, normal size. A B- setup is sized down, to 0.25% to 0.5%.

questions.simple: Cut his risk to 0.25% to 0.5%, because a B- setup is sized down, however big a month he wants.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, D38, A1)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Account $60,000. Our market reading is Green, so margin is allowed. What's the most all your positions together can be worth?
questions.why: $120,000. In a Green market, with margin, the book can run to 200% of the account: 200% of $60,000. In any other market the limit is 100%, the account itself, or $60,000 here. Margin is used only when our reading is Green. Risk per trade is still a percent of the account, not of the $120,000.
questions.lesson_line: Green market: the book can reach 200% on margin. Otherwise 100%.
questions.simple: All your positions can total $120,000, because a Green market allows 200% of a $60,000 account on margin.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7, B24, F60)
a computed key

questions.q: A full book of 10 positions at 200% of the account. About how big is the average position?
questions.why: About 20% of the account. A 200% book spread over 10 names averages 20% each. That is an average, not a rule: one position may reach the 40% cap while others sit smaller. Without margin the book is 100%, and 10 names would average 10%.
questions.lesson_line: Ten positions at a 200% book average about 20% each. The 40% cap is for one.

wrong.About 10% of the account: That's 100% over 10 names, the book without margin. In a Green market on margin it's 200%.
wrong.About 40% of the account: 40% is the cap on one position. Ten of those would be twice what the book allows.
wrong.About 2% of the account: 2% is the risk ceiling, a different number. Position size is how much you own, not how much you can lose.

questions.simple: About 20% each, because 200% spread over 10 positions works out to 20% per position.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A7)
a computed key

questions.story: You've been stopped out of the same stock three times this week. Those were your first tries on it this month. On Thursday it sets up again, cleaner than ever.
questions.q: Do you take the trade?
choices: Pass, the weekly limit is used
Pass, and drop it for the month
Take it, the setup is cleaner now
Take it, but at half the size
questions.answer: Pass, the weekly limit is used
questions.why: Pass. The same stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month. You've used this week's three, so a fourth try waits, however clean it looks. These were your first tries this month, so a later week still has tries left.
questions.lesson_line: Same stock: 3 tries a week, 6 a month. The fourth try waits.

wrong.Take it, the setup is cleaner now: The limit has no exception for a clean setup. This week's three tries are used.
wrong.Pass, and drop it for the month: Right to pass, wrong reason. The month allows 6 tries, and these were your first. A later week can try again.
wrong.Take it, but at half the size: Half size is still a fourth try. The rule counts tries, not shares.

questions.simple: Pass, because one stock gets at most 3 tries a week, and you have used all 3.

deeper.trap: The monthly limit is the quiet one. These three tries count toward the month's 6. Three more in a later week of the same month would use up all 6. A stock that keeps stopping you out uses up the month fast.

reasons: one cited fact only (h16)
rests on the owner's rulebook (E56)
a house number the owner set

questions.story: A small stock looks perfect: a tight base and a clean pivot. It trades at $14 and about $8 million a day.
questions.q: Is it a trade by our rules?
choices: No, $14 is too low a price
Yes, if you use a limit order
questions.why: No. We trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. At $14 it passes the price test, but $8 million a day fails the volume test. A stock must pass both. Illiquid stocks are not even watched. A thin stock can be hard to sell and hand you a bigger loss.
questions.lesson_line: Both tests, every time: $10 or more, and $20 million a day or more.

wrong.Yes, the price clears $10: Price is one test. Volume is the other, and $8 million a day fails it.
wrong.Yes, if you use a limit order: A limit order helps in a thin stock, but our rule keeps thin stocks off the list entirely.
wrong.No, $14 is too low a price: Wrong reason. $14 clears our $10 floor. The problem is $8 million a day, under our $20 million.

questions.simple: No, it fails our volume test, because it trades $8 million a day and we need at least $20 million.

deeper.counter: Dollar volume is the test that protects your exit. In a thin stock even a small order can be a big share of a day's trading and move the price. A full position here could be hard to sell when you need out, and hand you a bigger loss.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, D42)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: 2x and 3x ETFs are off limits under our rules.
questions.why: False. They are preferred under our rules, with no extra rules. Know the mechanics: a 2x or 3x fund aims for a multiple of its index's daily move. A 2x fund loses 2% for every 1% the index loses. Stop first, then the same share math.
questions.lesson_line: 2x and 3x ETFs are preferred here. Stop first, then the same share math.
questions.simple: False, 2x and 3x ETFs are preferred under our rules, with no extra rules for them.

deeper.trap: Preferred does not mean sized up. A 2x fund aims for twice its index's daily move, so it loses 2% for every 1% the index loses. The same share math still applies: the stop distance sets the shares, and the risk percent stays the same.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E54), which sits beside the SEC's daily-reset warnings (conflicts line)

questions.q: By our rules, the default stop goes exactly at the day's low, not under it.
questions.why: False. By default the stop goes a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, so it sits below the low, not on it. The stop comes first, and the size comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Default stop: a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.simple: False, the default stop goes a few cents under the low, not exactly on it.

deeper.trap: Your usual stop distance is a guide, not a rule that sets it. The stop goes a few cents under the day's low. If that low is far below your buy, the honest stop is wider. The share math then gives fewer shares, or you skip.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)

questions.q: Our line: "I almost never take a loss greater than 3%." 3% of what?
questions.why: The position's value. The stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy, so a planned stop-out costs about 3% of that position. The account's planned loss is your risk percent, 0.25% to 1.5% by grade, under the 2% ceiling. The share count links the two; they are not the same number.
questions.lesson_line: 3% is the stop's distance on the stock. The account's loss is your risk percent.

wrong.The account's total value: A 3% loss on the account would be above our 2% ceiling. The 3% is on the position.
wrong.Your margin buying power: Margin changes buying power, not where the stop sits. The 3% is on the stock you bought.
wrong.All your positions together: That's the whole book, up to 100% or 200% of the account. The 3% is one position's loss.

questions.simple: It means 3% of the position's value, since the stop sits near the buy. The account's planned loss is your risk percent.

deeper.trap: Reading 3% as account risk would put every trade above our 2% ceiling. Read it as the stop's width on one stock, from your buy to your stop. The account's loss is the risk percent you picked by grade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A13, E49, A1)
a house number taught as a guideline

questions.story: You set your sizes in January from a $50,000 account. It's June, the account is $62,000, and you still size from $50,000.
questions.q: What does our rule say?
questions.why: Recalculate weekly or monthly, either one, and size every trade from that number. Five months on a stale $50,000 is too long when the account is $62,000. With a fixed percent, your dollar risk grows with the account while the percent stays the same. It works both ways: a smaller account means smaller trades.
questions.lesson_line: Size from the account as it is, recalculated weekly or monthly.

wrong.Keep $50,000, it's conservative: Sizing small is fine, but it has to be a choice from the real number, not an old one.
wrong.Recalculate only after a drawdown: The account changes both ways. Our rule is a schedule, weekly or monthly, not a trigger.
wrong.Recalculate only at year end: Too seldom. Our rule is weekly or monthly, so a year-old number is far out of date.

questions.simple: Recalculate your account weekly or monthly, so each trade is sized from what the account is worth now.

deeper.trap: Here the account grew, so the old number only made you too small. If the account had fallen instead, sizing from the old, higher number would risk more than your percent on every trade. Recalculating keeps the percent honest in both directions.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D43)
a house schedule the owner set

questions.story: An A setup triggers. Your plan says 400 shares. You buy 200 now and plan to add the other 200 if it keeps working.
questions.q: What does our rule say?
choices: Buy all 400 now with one stop
Add the rest once it starts paying
Buy 200 now, 200 on a dip lower
questions.answer: Buy all 400 now with one stop
questions.why: Buy all 400 at one price with one stop. The full size goes on at once: no starter position and no adds, not on strength and not on a dip. The plan already sized 400 from the stop and the cap. If that full size does not fit the honest stop, the trade is smaller or it is a pass.
questions.lesson_line: Full size at one price with one stop. No pilot, no adds.

wrong.Add the rest once it starts paying: That's a pilot-then-add plan, and it isn't ours. Full size at one spot with one stop.
wrong.Buy 200 now, 200 on a dip lower: Adding below your buy is adding to a trade that's going against you. One price, one stop.
wrong.Buy all 400 with two stops: One price and one stop for the full size. Two stops split one trade into two plans.

questions.simple: Buy all 400 shares at one price with one stop, because we never scale in or add later.

deeper.trap: Buying more on a dip lower feels like a better price. It is adding to a trade that is going against you, under the same stop. Our rule is one price, one stop. If the full size is too big for the stop, buy fewer shares from the start.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A3)
fixed before (owner named in a wrong-note)

questions.story: Five winners in a row. You feel sharp. Our market reading is Green. The next setup is a B, and you want to risk 2% on it.
questions.q: What do our rules let you risk on it?
questions.why: 0.5% to 1%. A B setup is normal size, at 0.5% to 1% of the account. A run of winners never raises risk past the rules. 1.5% is the top of the A+ range, and 0.25% to 0.5% is for B- or lower. 2% is the absolute ceiling, and no grade uses it. The grade sets the risk; your streak does not.
questions.lesson_line: Winners don't raise the risk. The grade does, and a B is 0.5% to 1%.

wrong.2%, the ceiling: 2% is the absolute ceiling, and no grade uses it. A B setup sits at 0.5% to 1%.
wrong.0.25% to 0.5%, B range: That's the B- or lower range. A B setup is normal size, 0.5% to 1%.
wrong.1.5%, earned by streak: 1.5% is the top of the A+ range. A streak doesn't turn a B into an A+, and winners never raise risk past the rules.

questions.simple: You may risk 0.5% to 1%, because a B setup gets that range and a winning streak never raises it.

deeper.trap: A streak feels like proof you are sharp, and that is the moment this rule is written for. Five wins in a row do not change a B grade, and the grade sets the risk. Raising risk past the rules after winners is out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E49, D45, A1)
a house number the owner set

questions.q: Four experienced traders each describe one of their rules. Which one breaks ours?
choices: A 40% position on a tight stop
questions.why: 200% long in a Yellow market. Margin up to 200% is used only when our market reading is Green. In any other market, the book stays at 100% of the account. The other three sit inside our rules. A flat risk percent on every trade is allowed. 1.5% is the top of the A+ range. A position may reach the 40% cap.
questions.lesson_line: Margin to 200% only in a Green market. In every other reading, the book stays at 100%.

wrong.A 40% position on a tight stop: 40% is our cap, and a position may reach it. Only going past 40% breaks the rule.
wrong.Flat 0.5% risk on every trade: Flat risk, the same percent every trade, is fine under our rules. Pick one way and write it down.
wrong.1.5% risk on every A+ setup: That's the top of the A+ range. Inside the rules.

questions.simple: The 200% book in a Yellow market breaks our rules, because margin to 200% is used only when the reading is Green.

deeper.trap: A 200% book sounds bold, and in a Green market it is ours. The market reading decides it. In Yellow, Orange or Red, the book stays at 100% of the account.
